text: You're given an array nums of n plus one integers, where every integer is in the range one to n inclusive. There is exactly one repeated number. Return it. Two constraints: you must not modify the array, and you may only use constant extra space.

Let me make sure I have the shape right. The array has one more slot than there are possible values — n plus one slots, values drawn from one through n. So for one, three, four, two, two, that's five elements with values from one to four, and the answer is two. Two clarifications. First — can the duplicate appear more than twice? Like two, two, two, one, three?
Yes, it can. Only one value repeats, but it may repeat any number of times.

Good — that rules out anything that assumes exactly two occurrences. Second: is it guaranteed a duplicate exists at all? Actually, I can answer that myself. It's pigeonhole. I have n plus one items to place into n possible values, so at least one value is used twice. The extra guarantee — that only one value repeats — isn't needed for existence; it's what makes the answer unique.
That's the follow-up question, answered before I asked it. Go ahead.

Let me lay out the obvious approaches and let the constraints eliminate them. A hash set is linear time but linear space — it breaks the space rule. Sorting is n log n, and sorting in place modifies the array, while a sorted copy costs linear space. Negative marking flips signs at the indices the values point to — constant space, but the sign bits are the memory, so it modifies the array. Both constraints together block every remember-what-I've-seen strategy. That's the signal: I need something that doesn't record anything.
Do you have anything that survives both?

Yes — let me put a safe one on the table first, then try to beat it. Binary search on the value, not the index. Pick a midpoint value, then count how many elements are at most mid. Pigeonhole again: if that count exceeds mid, the duplicate lives in the left half. That's n log n time, constant space, and it only reads the array. Both constraints satisfied. But you'd probably ask for linear, so let me look for a better angle.
I would. Take a minute.

The values are in one to n, and the indices are in zero to n. So every value is itself a valid index — I can treat nums of i as a pointer. Define an edge from index i to index nums of i. Every node has exactly one outgoing edge, so this is a linked list whose next pointer is an array lookup. With finitely many nodes, walking from index zero must revisit one: there is a cycle. And the key detail: values are at least one, so no edge ever points at index zero. Index zero has no predecessor, so it's outside the cycle. The shape is a tail leading into a loop — a rho.
And how does that give you the duplicate?

The entrance to the cycle is the one node with two incoming edges — one from the tail, one from wrapping around the loop. Translate that back: an edge into node v means some index holds v. Two edges into v means two different indices hold the same value. That's the duplicate. So find the cycle entrance, and that's the answer. This problem reminds me of finding where a linked list's cycle begins — Floyd's tortoise and hare fits exactly, with p's next replaced by nums of p.

Let me walk one, three, four, two, two first. From index zero, the walk goes one, three, then two, four, two, four — a tail of three into a cycle of length two, entering at two, the repeated value. Here's the plan. One: start slow and fast together at nums of zero. Two: slow moves one step, fast moves two, until they meet — somewhere on the cycle, not necessarily the entrance; in this example they happen to coincide, which is misleading. Three: reset slow to the start, leave fast at the meeting point, move both one step at a time; where they meet is the entrance.
Why does phase two land on the entrance? Don't just tell me it works.

Measure from where both pointers start. Let mu be the distance to the entrance, lambda the cycle length, and d the steps slow has taken when they meet. Fast has taken two d, on the same node, so the difference d is a whole number of laps. Walking mu steps from the start lands on the entrance by definition. Walking mu steps from the meeting point is like walking d plus mu from the start, and the d is whole laps, so it cancels out. Both reach the entrance after exactly mu steps — which is why they must move at the same speed.

Alright, here's the code. Two things to call out. The do-while is not stylistic. Both pointers start at nums of zero, so they're already equal. A plain while would skip the loop, phase two would skip too, and the function degenerates into return nums of zero. And the double index needs no bounds check: every value is in one to n, and the array has indices zero through n, so both lookups are provably in range — and there's no null to guard.
Trace it on your example.

One, three, four, two, two — expected two. The row that matters is round two of phase one: slow and fast meet at two, which here is also the entrance — a coincidence of this input. Stopping after phase one would pass this test and fail others. Phase two resets slow, and two rounds later they meet at two again. Returns two. Correct. Edge case: the smallest legal input, one, one. They meet at one in phase one, and phase two finds them already equal. Returns one. Correct.
What if I told you a candidate wrote this with a plain while, and it passed most of their own tests?

I'd believe it, and that's the worst kind of bug — it just returns nums of zero, which is the right answer surprisingly often: about forty-four percent of all small inputs up to n equals six. The shortest input that exposes it is one, two, two — it returns one instead of two. The general lesson: if two pointers start at the same node, test-then-move is a no-op. Either move first, or stagger the starting positions.

Time is linear: phase one is bounded by tail plus cycle length, phase two by the tail, and both are at most n. Space is constant — two integers. The array is never written to. So both constraints hold, and the linear follow-up is answered. One honest caveat: this leans hard on the values being one to n, not zero to n minus one. If zero were legal, index zero could sit inside the cycle and the rho shape is gone. Zero, one, one breaks it — index zero is a self-loop, and it returns zero instead of one. Then I'd fall back to the binary search on values, which doesn't care where the range starts.

Good session. Three things I'll note. You let the constraints do the work — you listed the obvious approaches and showed exactly which constraint killed each one. You put a correct, slower solution on the table first, so even out of time you'd have an answer that meets every requirement. And you knew which condition your solution depends on. Many people can recite Floyd's; fewer can tell me that values start at one is the load-bearing sentence, and hand me the input that breaks it.
